title: Serving runtime handbook and playbooks
author: Ava Martinez
summary: Consolidated handbook for the Serving Runtime team: architecture overview, kernel scheduling design, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite, release guidance, known issues, and on-call runbooks. This document is the canonical starting point for engineering, SRE, and support when diagnosing performance, planning releases, or onboarding new team members.
body:
Purpose and scope

This handbook consolidates the day-to-day operational knowledge for Redwood's Serving Runtime. It covers: architecture and data flow, kernel and scheduling strategies, profiling/playbooks for perf debugging, our benchmarking suite and how to run it, release and upgrade procedures, a catalog of known issues with mitigations, and the primary runbooks used by oncall and incident responders.

Audience
- Serving runtime engineers
- Eng SRE and capacity planners
- Platform/infra teams integrating with the runtime
- Support/Customer Success for escalations requiring runtime-level investigation

1) Runtime architecture (high-level)

Intro
The serving runtime is a GPU-optimized inference engine that provides token-level execution for transformer models, a cache-aware request router, and integration points for quantized kernels. The runtime is separated into three logical layers: Transport & Ingress, Scheduler & Executor, and Model Kernel Layer.

Components
- Transport & Ingress: HTTP/gRPC endpoint, load balancer, request pre-processor (batch keying, tokenization hints). Responsible for auth, quota, and initial routing policy decisions.
- Scheduler & Executor: Continuous-batching scheduler, KV cache manager, session manager, kernel selector. Implements SLO-aware scheduling and backpressure.
- Model Kernel Layer: Collection of device-native kernels (CUDA, ROCm, and CPU fallback), quantized paths (8-bit/4-bit), attention optimizations, and fast softmax primitives.

Data flow (short):
1. Request arrives -> validated and annotated with routing policy (latency-optimized, cost-optimized, or region-specific).
2. Request enters scheduling queue and is assigned a session with KV cache metadata.
3. Scheduler groups compatible requests into a batch; kernel selector picks the optimal kernel variant based on model, seq_len, and hardware.
4. Executor runs kernels, updates KV cache, and streams tokens back through transport.

SLOs and metrics (owner: eng-sre)
- P50 latency (single-token generation) by model tier: <= 25ms (latency tier), <= 50ms (balanced tier).
- P95 latency: <= 120ms (latency tier), <= 200ms (balanced tier).
- Availability: 99.95% per region for hosted; dedicated customers have contractual SLA documented elsewhere.
- Token throughput: monitored via tokens/sec per GPU, target ranges published per machine-type in the capacity doc.

Primary observability signals
- per-route latency histograms, per-model kernel-selection ratios, batch size distribution, queue depth per scheduling pool, KV cache hit-rate, GPU SM utilization, memory occupancy, and per-request trace IDs.

2) Kernel selection and scheduling design

Goals
- Minimize tail latency while maximizing aggregate tokens/sec and utilization.
- Prefer fast-path kernels when sequence lengths and precision allow.
- Enable graceful degradation to CPU/compat kernels when GPU resources are constrained.

Scheduling tiers and pools
- Latency pool: small batches (1-4), prioritized preemption, strict per-request SLO enforcement.
- Balanced pool: medium batches (4-16), throughput-oriented with soft latency targets.
- Throughput pool: large batches (>16), cost-optimized and typically for background or batch workloads.

Kernel selection rules (simplified)
1. If seq_len <= 64 and model supports fused attention -> choose fused fast-path kernel (8-bit if compatible).
2. If KV cache hit-rate high and session warm -> allow larger batch composition for amortized kernel launch cost.
3. For long sequences (>512) prefer chunked-attention kernels to avoid O(N^2) explosion in memory; fall back to CPU kernel if GPU memory risk exceeds safety threshold.
4. If GPU memory usage > 85% trigger admission control to queue new large-seq requests or route to other regions/variants.

Admission and backpressure
- Admission controller enforces per-GPU concurrent token cap: configurable per machine-type. Default: 1.2M tokens concurrent for A100-80GB equivalent.
- If queue depth > queue_depth_high (default 150) for >10s, triggered policy: expand balanced pool replicas, degrade to smaller batch sizes in latency pool, and publish metric alert.

3) Profiling playbook (performance debugging)

Overview: This is the step-by-step playbook for diagnosing a runtime performance regression (increased latency, reduced throughput, or higher error rates). Target audience: oncall, runtime engineers, and SREs.

Quick triage (first 10 minutes)
1. Check cluster health dashboard: GPU count, node status, OOMs, driver/firmware alerts.
2. Inspect per-route latency and top-5 slowest models in the last 15m.
3. Find a representative trace ID for a slow request (use trace sampling or request ID from customer).
4. Run fast checks: kernel-selection distribution, batch-size histogram, queue depth, and KV cache hit-rate for the affected pool.

Deeper diagnosis (10-60 minutes)
1. Kernel-level profiling: enable sampling profiler on one replica (sampling to avoid adding overhead). Command example: "runtime-profiler --target <pod> --duration 60s --sampling 10ms --output /tmp/profile.pb".
2. GPU metrics: collect nvidia-smi and DCGM snapshots: "nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,utilization.memory,memory.used --format=csv -l 1 -f /tmp/gpu.csv".
3. Check for SM stalls: use DCGM or CUPTI traces to detect memcopy or kernel launch stalls.
4. Kernel runtime breakdown: inspect profiler output to compute percent time spent in attention, softmax, matmul, and memory copies.

Common root causes and remediations
- Symptom: sudden P95 jump, SM utilization low -> likely kernel launch churn (too many tiny batches). Remediation: increase batch window or route affected traffic to balanced pool.
- Symptom: large memory spikes and OOMs -> long sequence requests or a model with memory leak. Remediation: enable chunked attention or temporarily reduce concurrent token cap.
- Symptom: shift to CPU kernels (slower) -> GPU driver crash/restart or missing kernel artifact. Remediation: check node events and rebuild kernel cache on node.
- Symptom: KV cache hit-rate drop -> cache invalidation or session mismatch. Remediation: validate session affinity and check cache eviction policies.

Profiling playbook appendix: commands and artifact collection
- Collect traces: "curl -H 'x-request-id: <trace>' https://runtime-host/route?trace=1 -o /tmp/trace.json"
- Upload artifacts to s3 for postmortem: "aws s3 cp /tmp/profile.pb s3://redwood-runtime-artifacts/<incident-id>/"
- Required artifacts for postmortem: profiler output, GPU snapshots, representative request payload, kernel selection logs, and scheduler queue logs.

4) Benchmarking suite (how-to and interpretation)

Bench goals
- Measure per-GPU tokens/sec and latency for representative models (e.g., gpt-small, gpt-medium, llama-13B, and rlhf-tuned variants).
- Validate kernel performance across sequence-lengths and batch sizes.
- Regression detection: automated nightly runs with baseline comparisons and alerting on >5% throughput drop or >10% latency increase at P95.

How to run locally (dev)
- Checkout: "git clone git@github.com:redwood-inference/serving-benchmarks.git"
- Example command: "bench-runner --model llm-13b --gpu-type a100-80 --batch-sizes 1,4,8,16 --seq-lens 32,128,512 --out /tmp/bench-llm-13b.json"
- The runner will produce a normalized report with: batch-size -> avg latency, p50, p95, tokens/sec, kernel variants used.

Nightly CI and alerting
- Nightly jobs run in dedicated perf cluster. Results stored in timeseries and compared against rolling baseline. If regression triggers, the perf-signal channel is auto-notified and a perf triage ticket created.

Interpreting results
- Focus on tokens/sec delta for throughput-oriented workloads and p95 delta for latency-sensitive workloads.
- Correlate kernel variant shifts (e.g., fallbacks to safe-path) with regressions; look for infra changes (driver bump, CUDA, ROCm).

5) Release notes and upgrade guidance (runtime binaries and kernel artifacts)

Release cadence
- Minor patches: weekly (bugfixes and small perf improvements).
- Major feature releases: quarterly (kernel changes, scheduler upgrades).

Release checklist (pre-release)
- Confirm benchmarks (nightly run) show no regressions vs baseline.
- Validate upgrade path on staging and a single dedicated cluster.
- Smoke tests: end-to-end inference, streaming, KV cache warm startup, and failover tests.
- Docs: update runbooks and kernel compatibility matrix.

Upgrade steps (on-prem and dedicated customers)
1. Create release candidate image and run canary on 1% of traffic for 24 hours.
2. Monitor kernel-selection ratios, per-model p95 latency, and OOMs.
3. If stable, ramp canary to 10%, then 50% over incremental windows.
4. For dedicated/private fleets, coordinate with customer ops and schedule maintenance windows.

Rollback criteria
- >5% sustained P95 regression for 30 minutes, >1% error rate increase, or any OOM causing node loss.

6) Known issues (catalog and mitigations)

Issue: intermittent kernel fallback to CPU after driver update
- Symptom: sudden increase in latency for certain models and kernel logs show missing kernel image.
- Root cause: driver ABI mismatch with precompiled kernel cache.
- Mitigation: rebuild kernel cache on nodes using "runtime-kernel-cache --rebuild" and coordinate driver rollback if necessary.

Issue: batcher starvation under bursty small requests
- Symptom: low GPU utilization and high P95 due to many single-token requests arriving unsynchronised.
- Mitigation: enable micro-batching with 5ms delay in latency pool or apply front-door request coalescing in the ingress layer.

Issue: KV cache thrash after session affinity changes
- Symptom: repeated cold starts for sessions and high average latency for affected users.
- Mitigation: restore sticky routing, increase cache size for warm sessions, and add proactive prefetch for top-N users.

7) Runbooks (oncall playbooks)

Runbook: P95 latency increase for model X
1. Identify affected replicas and sample traces.
2. Verify if regression is kernel-level or scheduler-level (use profiler and batch histograms).
3. If due to tiny batches: change pool config to allow slightly larger batching window: "POST /api/config/pools/latency -d '{\"batch_window_ms\":8}'".
4. If due to memory pressure: decrease concurrent token cap: "runtime-config set concurrent_token_cap=800000" and notify capacity.
5. If not resolved in 30m, execute rollback to previous runtime image following release rollback SOP.

Runbook: node OOM or GPU crash
1. Isolate node and mark unschedulable: "kubectl cordon <node>".
2. Collect /var/log/messages, dmesg, and kernel logs, and the runtime core dump if present.
3. Redeploy workload to healthy nodes and file incident for driver/firmware investigation.
4. If OOM is reproducible on multiple nodes, add emergency admission control to reduce concurrent_token_cap cluster-wide.

8) Team wiki and onboarding checklist

New engineer checklist (first 2 weeks)
- Read this handbook and related architecture docs.
- Execute the local benchmark (bench-runner) and review results with a teammate.
- Run profiler and analyze a sample trace; submit a one-pager on findings.
- Shadow oncall for at least 2 rotations.

Important links and artifacts
- Kernel compatibility matrix: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-compatibility-matrix
- Benchmark results dashboard: https://perf.redwood.internal/dashboards/serving-runtime
- Artifact bucket for profiler outputs: s3://redwood-runtime-artifacts/

9) Post-incident and continuous improvement

- Every Sev2+ incident must include the collected profiling artifacts and a perf-regression check.
- Perf triage meeting weekly to review regressions and assign owners to remediate kernel-level and scheduler-level causes.
- Maintain a small internal blacklist of workloads that consistently cause instability; owners must propose remediation plans (model changes, batching hints, or resource isolation).

Appendix: example configurations and quick references

Admission controller config (example YAML snippet described in text):
- concurrent_token_cap: 1200000
- queue_depth_high: 150
- batch_window_ms: { latency_pool: 5, balanced_pool: 10, throughput_pool: 25 }

Common CLI snippets
- Rebuild kernel cache: "runtime-kernel-cache --rebuild --node <node-name>"
- Snapshot scheduler queues: "curl -s http://scheduler-service/admin/queues | jq '.' > /tmp/queues.json"
- Run profiler (sampling): "runtime-profiler --target <pod> --duration 60s --sampling 10ms --output /tmp/profile.pb"

Contact and ownership
- Runtime team leads: Ava Martinez (owner), Daniel Chu (kernel and scheduling), Priya Nair (profiling & perf).
- Eng SRE (support): Liam O'Connor.
